If asked to present your findings:

"This is a 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+2 weeks' gestation presenting with regular uterine contractions occurring approximately every 5 minutes. She is haemodynamically stable and afebrile. There is no vaginal bleeding or history of fluid leakage. The uterus is soft and non-tender between contractions. Fetal heart rate is 145 beats per minute with reassuring fetal movements and CTG findings. Speculum examination shows no pooling of liquor and the cervix appears closed. There are no clinical features of infection or placental abruption. At present, this is suspicious for threatened preterm labour, and I would complete assessment with appropriate cervical assessment and investigations."

"This is a 29-year-old primigravida at 31 weeks presenting with regular painful contractions. She is haemodynamically stable and afebrile. The fetal heart rate is reassuring. There is no vaginal bleeding or evidence of ruptured membranes. Speculum examination shows an apparently closed cervix, with no pooling of liquor. There is currently no evidence of progressive cervical dilatation, therefore this is more consistent with threatened rather than established preterm labour."

"This is a 28-year-old G2P1 at 29+4 weeks with regular painful contractions occurring every 3 minutes. She is haemodynamically stable and afebrile. The fetal heart rate is currently reassuring. There is no significant vaginal bleeding. The membranes appear intact. Vaginal examination demonstrates a cervix that is 4 cm dilated and approximately 80% effaced with progressive cervical change. These findings are consistent with established preterm labour. I would involve the senior obstetric and neonatal teams, administer antenatal corticosteroids, consider tocolysis if there are no contraindications, assess the indication for magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, and plan the mode and timing of delivery according to maternal and fetal condition."

"This is a 30-year-old G2P1 at 31 weeks presenting with regular contractions and continuous leakage of clear vaginal fluid. She is currently haemodynamically stable and afebrile. There is no significant vaginal bleeding. Speculum examination demonstrates pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix consistent with ruptured membranes. I would assess for infection, fetal wellbeing and labour, involve the neonatal team and manage this as preterm labour with PPROM."

subsections.subsection_title: REPORTING — PRETERM LABOUR WITH SUSPECTED CHORIOAMNIONITIS

blocks.text: "This is a 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks with established preterm labour who is febrile at 38.5°C, tachycardic and has uterine tenderness. The fetal heart rate is elevated at 175 beats per minute. There is offensive vaginal fluid. These findings are concerning for intrauterine infection/chorioamnionitis. I would initiate maternal sepsis management, obtain appropriate cultures and investigations, commence appropriate antibiotics and involve the senior obstetric and neonatal teams. Tocolysis would not be appropriate if infection is confirmed or strongly suspected."

subsections.subsection_title: REPORTING — PRETERM LABOUR WITH PLACENTAL ABRUPTION

blocks.text: "This is a 32-week pregnant woman presenting with painful regular contractions and vaginal bleeding. She is tachycardic and hypotensive. The uterus is tender and hypertonic, with frequent contractions, and the CTG demonstrates significant fetal compromise. This is highly concerning for placental abruption with established preterm labour and fetal compromise. I would initiate immediate maternal resuscitation, activate the major obstetric haemorrhage pathway if indicated, involve senior obstetric and anaesthetic teams and proceed to urgent delivery after maternal stabilisation."

"This is a 25-week pregnant woman with regular painful contractions and progressive cervical dilatation. The membranes are intact and there is no evidence of infection or significant bleeding. The fetus is currently viable with a reassuring heart rate. This represents very preterm established labour. I would urgently involve maternal-fetal medicine and neonatology, discuss prognosis and options with the patient, administer antenatal corticosteroids where appropriate, consider magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection, consider tocolysis if appropriate and arrange delivery/transfer in a facility with appropriate neonatal intensive care."

items: "How would you manage this woman with suspected preterm labour?"

blocks.text: "I would first assess the mother and fetus, confirm the gestational age and assess for maternal or fetal compromise. I would take a focused history regarding contractions, vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, fetal movements, infection symptoms and previous preterm birth. I would check maternal observations and perform an abdominal examination assessing uterine activity, tenderness, fetal lie and presentation, followed by fetal heart-rate assessment. I would perform a sterile speculum examination where appropriate to assess the cervix, bleeding and whether the membranes are intact, with digital examination only when necessary.

I would investigate with appropriate maternal blood tests, urinalysis and cultures where indicated, and use CTG and ultrasound as appropriate. In women ≥30 weeks with suspected preterm labour, transvaginal cervical-length assessment can help determine the likelihood of birth within 48 hours, with fetal fibronectin an alternative when cervical-length assessment is unavailable or unacceptable under the NICE pathway.

If preterm birth is likely, I would involve the senior obstetrician and neonatal team, arrange transfer if appropriate, administer antenatal corticosteroids according to gestation, consider or offer nifedipine tocolysis when appropriate and membranes are intact, and consider magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection at very preterm gestations. I would not use tocolysis where there is significant bleeding, infection, fetal compromise or another indication for immediate delivery. Finally, I would determine the timing and mode of delivery according to maternal and fetal condition and the obstetric circumstances." NICE
